Need to search first.I couldn't cover the whole chapter. The search tool hit its usage limit partway through, and full-page fetches failed. What follows comes from search-result excerpts of the pages listed, so some pages were only partly read. I found nothing usable for vv. 12–14, 17–18, 20, 22–23, 27, 31 or 36. I also have nothing on point 3's Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran or Wesleyan readings, prosperity or hyper-grace teaching, or bibleodyssey and netbible notes. Those gaps are left out, not filled in.

**Chapter overview**
- David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic-leaning) describes Josiah's reform as a return to God's Word, an Old Testament picture of *sola scriptura* (the Reformation principle of "Scripture alone"). He also says it stayed largely outward: Jeremiah's preaching in those same years shows the people's hearts never really turned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/
- Matthew Henry: Josiah had been told ruin couldn't be prevented, but he didn't give up. He did his duty and left the outcome to God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_023.cfm

**v. 1:** Guzik: Josiah wasn't content just to escape judgment in his own lifetime. He knew he couldn't put the kingdom right alone, so he called in the elders to repent with him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/

**v. 2:** The Pulpit Commentary stresses how highly the king honoured the book by reading every word himself to a nation that had long ignored it. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-23.html. Precept Austin quotes John Walton: since most people couldn't read, public readings mattered a great deal, and Assyrian heralds read royal decrees aloud at city gates. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-23-commentary

**v. 3:**
- **The pillar.** Readings differ:
  - A royal platform: Clarke and Gill link it to the bronze platform Solomon used (2 Chron 6:13). Barnes reads "upon the pillar." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/23-3.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-3.htm
  - Coffman, citing Peake, thinks it was Jachin or Boaz, the two great pillars at the temple front. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-kings-23.html
  - Walton (via Precept Austin) says no clear parallel to this custom exists elsewhere in the ancient Near East. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-23-commentary
- **The covenant.**
  - Barnes says Josiah renewed the Horeb covenant (Deut 5:2) on behalf of the whole nation. Benson says the king covenanted first, as an example. Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary says most of the people were going through the motions or were hypocritical, yet the covenant still checked open wickedness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-3.htm
  - Coffman: this was a renewed promise to keep the old covenant, not a new one. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-kings-23.html
  - Guzik notes that "made a covenant" is literally "cut a covenant," from the practice of walking between halves of a sacrificed animal (Gen 15). He says the people's response was spontaneous, a work of God that came through the king's example. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/
  - G. Campbell Morgan (via Precept Austin): the people were simply following the king, with no real repentance. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-23-commentary

**v. 4:**
- Guzik: idols stood in the temple itself, which shows how deep the idolatry went. Josiah cleaned from the centre outward. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/
- **Why the ashes went to Bethel.**
  - Poole, Gill, Benson and Keil & Delitzsch say it was to defile and disgrace Bethel, the chief seat of idolatry since Jeroboam.
  - Ellicott finds it strange that only these ashes went there and suspects the text is corrupt.
  - The Pulpit Commentary takes it as a sign of Josiah's extreme scrupulousness.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-4.htm

**v. 5:**
- **"Idolatrous priests" (kemarim).**
  - Ellicott takes them as unlawful priests of the LORD, as distinct from Baal's priests.
  - Barnes calls them non-Levitical high-place priests and thinks the word is a foreign term.
  - Benson reports the view that the name comes from black robes.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-5.htm
- **A side debate over clergy dress.** Clarke and Coffman both use the "black-robed priest" idea to criticise black clerical clothing today. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/23-5.html
- Guzik: real reform has to remove the people who promote sin, not just the objects. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/
- GotQuestions: these may have claimed to serve the LORD while actually sacrificing to other gods. https://www.gotquestions.org/Chemarim-Chemarims.html

**v. 6:** Barnes: the dust was scattered on graves because graves were already unclean. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-4.htm

**v. 7:** Guzik: so-called sacred prostitution was central to these cults, and the temple had become a brothel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/

**v. 8:**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): "Geba to Beersheba" means from the north to the south of Judah. The altars at the governor's gate may have been to the true God, but they broke His rules for worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-9.htm
- Coffman: God had ordered the high places destroyed (Num 33:52) because they couldn't be cleansed of their fertility-cult associations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/23-9.html

**v. 9:**
- Benson, Poole, Barnes and Clarke agree on the main reading. These priests had worshipped the true God in forbidden places. They were barred from the altar but still fed from priestly portions, like priests with a physical defect (Lev 21:17–22). Poole and Benson call this mercy mixed with severity.
- Ellicott instead thinks they ate apart from the legitimate priests.
- Sources: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-9.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/23-9.html
- A BibleHub Q&A ties the verse to centralised worship (Deut 12) and to Ezekiel 44's demotion of unfaithful Levites. https://biblehub.com/q/2_Kings_23_9_on_worship_centralization.htm

**v. 10:**
- **Child sacrifice.** Gill and the rabbis cited by Clarke say drums drowned out the children's cries, which is where "Topheth" got its name. The Pulpit Commentary and Keil & Delitzsch prefer a root meaning "to spit": a place to be spat at. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/23-10.html
- **Burned or "passed through" the fire?** Benson reports that many think children were only dedicated by passing them between fires, not burned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-10.htm
- Gill and the Pulpit Commentary: "Ge-Hinnom" (the Valley of Hinnom) is where the New Testament word *Gehenna* (hell) comes from. Henry says Josiah made it the city's burial ground. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-10.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/23-10.html
- Guzik: Molech worship had lasted from Manasseh until Josiah. https://enduringword.com/choosing-bad-examples/

**v. 11:** Ellicott: real horses pulled the sun-god's chariots in processions and were kept in the outer court. He rejects the idea that this was a bronze artwork. Benson notes that several ancient nations dedicated horses to the sun because they are swift. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/23-11.htm

**v. 15:** Guzik: Josiah could act in the old northern kingdom because Assyria was weak. Patterson and Austel think purely Canaanite worship had by then replaced the golden calf at Bethel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/

**v. 16:** The Pulpit Commentary treats the man of God from Judah as a lone witness for truth, finally proved right centuries later. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-23.html

**v. 19:** Guzik: the reform reached the cities of Samaria as well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/

**v. 20:** Henry calls the slaying of the high-place priests on their own altars the most acceptable sacrifice ever made there, offered to God's justice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/23-8.html

**v. 21:** Guzik: Josiah couldn't command heart obedience, but he could restore the Passover. Neglecting it showed the people had forgotten God's redemption. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/

**v. 24:** Guzik: this is the clearest example of the *sola scriptura* principle. Even so, judgment came soon after, which shows the conformity was outward. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/

**v. 25:** Henry: Josiah's religion was "heart-work," with right motives and aims. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_023.cfm

**v. 26:**
- Guzik: wrath wasn't turned aside because the people still loved Manasseh's sins. He quotes Morgan: knowing the reform wouldn't last didn't excuse Josiah from following the light he had. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/
- GotQuestions: the judgment was postponed (not cancelled) because of Josiah's godliness (2 Kings 22:20). https://www.gotquestions.org/Josiah-in-the-Bible.html

**vv. 29–30: Josiah's death, the clearest disagreement among the traditional teachers**
- **Guzik:** stubborn disobedience. Neco's warning really came from God (2 Chron 35), and Josiah ignored it. The battle site was probably Hadadrimmon (Zech 12:11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/ ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/
- **Matthew Henry:** Josiah had no clear call to fight and didn't consult God. Some think he lost the promise of dying "in peace." Henry himself thinks the promise was kept: he died at peace with God and didn't see Jerusalem fall. His death was still a rebuke for rashness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_023.cfm
- **BibleHub Q&A pages:** zeal without discernment. One also argues the Hebrew idiom of being gathered to one's grave "in peace" allows for death in battle. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Josiah_defy_God_s_warning.htm ; https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Pharaoh_Neco_kill_Josiah.htm
- **BibleHub Study Bible:** treats the death as foretold (2 Kings 22:20) and as a type of Christ, a righteous king dying in battle. https://biblehub.com/study/2_kings/23-29.htm
- **Critical view:** a commentator quoted on BibleHub's 2 Chronicles 35:20 page sees "two traditions." Kings' wording suggests a meeting, not a battle, so Josiah may have been killed at an interview, while Chronicles has him wounded in battle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/35-20.htm

**v. 32:** Guzik: Jehoahaz, a younger son, was the people's choice, not God's man. https://enduringword.com/loving-or-hating-gods-word/. Henry thinks the people picked him as more warlike, likely to avenge his father, rather than to continue the reform. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_023.cfm

**vv. 33–35:** Precept Austin sees divine judgment here in three ways. Judah loses its independence, since Egypt now picks its king. And the first Davidic king is taken away, a preview of the later exiles. (The excerpt cut off before the third.) https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-23-commentary. Henry says Neco turned against Josiah's family because Josiah had opposed him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_023.cfm

**v. 37:** Guzik contrasts Josiah, who honoured God's Word, with his son Jehoiakim, who burned it. https://enduringword.com/loving-or-hating-gods-word/. The Pulpit Commentary makes the same contrast: God's Word outlasted the king who tried to destroy it. That passage also takes a swipe at Rome for keeping Scripture from the people. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-23.html. Guzik quotes Trapp: Jehoiakim also killed the prophet Urijah (Jer 26). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-23/

**Where the traditions differ**
I found no clear split between Baptist, Methodist, Reformed or Lutheran readings in what I could read. The real disagreements were these:
- whether Josiah sinned at Megiddo (Guzik versus Henry's softer view, above);
- whether the priests in v. 9 ate with the other priests or apart;
- Coffman's argument against the critical idea that Deuteronomy was written in Josiah's day, which shows that debate exists. I couldn't reach the scholarly sources that argue it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/23-5.html
